title: The Failing Farm
realOrConstructed: Real history and science; Abi's assignment is invented
bigUnderstanding: Food is a system: crop, soil, water, timing, tools, knowledge and labor. The English failed because they brought the wrong crops, farmed the wrong ground the wrong way at the wrong time, without the people or knowledge to do it, during a drought. The Powhatan succeeded with crops and methods refined over generations, including corn, beans and squash planted together, which work as a living system. Sets up why Jamestown depended on Powhatan corn in the simulation.

opening.intro: 1609. Jamestown is starving. A few miles upriver, a Powhatan town has so much corn it trades the extra. Same sun. Same rain. So why is one field dying while the other one is full?

cards.label: The English field
cards.text: Neat rows of wheat and barley from England. Thin, yellow, patchy. Bare dirt baked hard between the rows.

cards.label: The Powhatan field
cards.text: Looks messy: corn in little hills, beans climbing the stalks, giant squash leaves covering the ground. And it's loaded with food.

cards.label: Your job
cards.text: The Virginia Company sent you to find out why its colony can't feed itself. They're paying. They want answers.

cards.label: How to win
cards.text: Explain why the English fields fail and the Powhatan fields thrive: at least 3 causes, each backed by evidence.

opening.prompt: What do you want to check first?

facilitatorNotes: This is a SOLVED case with several real causes. A strong answer names at least 3, backed by evidence. Bonus if she sees the Powhatan field works as a system (each plant helps the others).

Science is the star here. When she digs into beans or squash, let her figure out the mechanism: what nodules do, why shade keeps soil damp, why corn needs lots of nitrogen. Explain only what she needs.
Treat Powhatan farmers, mostly women, as experts with generations of knowledge, not as 'simple' or 'natural.' Their system was sophisticated technology.
Kemps and Tassore were Powhatan men held captive at Jamestown when they taught the English to plant corn. If she asks, be honest about that.
The rats evidence is about stored food, not the fields. If she uses it to explain failing fields, let her notice the difference.
Abi may know about fertilizer from earlier work. Don't remind her; let her connect it herself.
Pin real events to her timeline as they come up.
justInTimeConcepts: Nitrogen: a nutrient plants need to grow; corn uses a lot.
Nitrogen fixation: bacteria in bean root nodules turn nitrogen from the air into plant food.
Evaporation: bare, sunny soil dries out fast; shade slows it.
Native crops: plants bred over thousands of years to suit a place.
scaffolds: Compare the two fields one thing at a time: crop, ground, method, people, timing.
What does each plant in the Powhatan field do for the others?
Who actually did the farming in each place, and how much did they know?
completion: Abi has examined at least 3 pieces of evidence and explained, in her own words, at least 3 causes for the difference, each backed by evidence.

endReveal.concept: Agriculture as a system. Corn, beans and squash grown together (often called the Three Sisters) support each other: corn is the pole, beans feed the soil nitrogen, squash shades and protects the ground.

data.question: Why are the English fields at Jamestown failing while Powhatan fields nearby thrive?
data.winCondition: Explain why the English fields fail and the Powhatan fields thrive: at least 3 causes, each backed by evidence.
data.trueExplanation: Several causes together. (1) Wrong crops: English wheat and barley suit cool, wet England; corn was bred for this land and gives far more food per seed. (2) Wrong ground: Jamestown Island is low, marshy and salty in places; Powhatan fields sit on better-drained ground. (3) Wrong method: bare rows dry out and grow weeds; the Powhatan system of corn, beans and squash in hills keeps soil fertile (bean nodules add nitrogen), shaded and damp, with fewer weeds, and needs no plow. (4) Knowledge and labor: Powhatan women were expert farmers; many English were gentlemen who wouldn't farm, few were farmers, and men were sent hunting gold. (5) Timing: the English planted late. (6) A severe drought hurt everyone, but the Powhatan system handled it better. When colonists learned Powhatan methods in 1609, they grew corn successfully.
causalChain: English crops from a cool, wet country
In bare rows that dry out
By few farmers who knew this land

evidence.label: Inspect the English field up close
evidence.result: Wheat and barley from England in straight rows. Stunted, yellowing leaves. The bare soil between rows is cracked and hard. Weeds are winning in places. Some low corners are soggy and the plants there have rotted.

evidence.label: Inspect the Powhatan field up close
evidence.result: Corn planted in small mounds about a step apart. Bean vines spiral up the corn stalks. Big squash leaves spread across the ground between mounds. Hardly any bare dirt shows, and there are few weeds.

evidence.label: Compare the ground under each field
evidence.result: Jamestown Island is low and marshy. After rain, parts flood; near the river the soil tastes salty. The Powhatan field is on higher, well-drained ground by a creek, dark and crumbly.

evidence.label: Dig up a bean plant and look at its roots
evidence.result: The roots are covered in small lumps called nodules. Inside them live bacteria that take nitrogen from the air and turn it into a form plants can use as food. Corn is a hungry plant that uses up lots of nitrogen.

evidence.label: Check the soil under the squash leaves vs. bare soil
evidence.result: Under the squash leaves the soil is cooler and still damp. Bare soil in the English field is hot and dry. Prickly squash stems also discourage animals, and the shade blocks weed seedlings.

evidence.label: Where each crop comes from
evidence.result: Wheat and barley come from cool, rainy places like England. Corn was bred by Native farmers over thousands of years from a wild grass, and suits hot, humid Virginia summers. One planted corn kernel can produce hundreds of new kernels; wheat produces far fewer per seed.

evidence.label: Who does the farming in each place
evidence.result: In Powhatan towns, women are the farmers: skilled, organized, and trained from childhood by older women. Men clear new fields, hunt and fish. At Jamestown, many colonists are gentlemen who refuse to farm, there are few trained farmers, and men have been sent to hunt gold.

evidence.label: What tools each side uses
evidence.result: The English farm like they did at home, with rows meant for plows and oxen, but they have almost no plows and no work animals yet, just hoes and spades. Powhatan farmers use hoes and digging sticks; their mound method was designed for hand tools.

evidence.label: When each side planted
evidence.result: The English arrived in May 1607 and spent the first weeks building the fort, so crops went in late. Powhatan farmers plant in spring, in stages, so harvests come in over the summer and fall.

evidence.label: How the Powhatan prepare a field
evidence.result: Men kill trees by cutting a ring through the bark, then burn the brush. The ash enriches the soil. After several years, they let a field rest and recover while they farm a new one.

evidence.label: Tree-ring data for 1606–1612
evidence.result: Tree rings show the driest seven-year stretch in about 770 years in this region. Everyone's harvests were hurt, Powhatan and English.

evidence.label: What happened when the English copied Powhatan methods
evidence.result: In 1609 two Powhatan men held at Jamestown, Kemps and Tassore, showed the colonists how to plant corn their way. John Smith reported the colony planted 30 to 40 acres of corn that year.

evidence.label: What happened to the colony's stored corn
evidence.result: In 1609 the colonists opened their corn storage and found much of it eaten or spoiled by rats that came over on English ships.
